title: Promises

post.author: u/cadwallader_nights_yvaine
post.title: I'm the night director at a funeral home. Our streaming company's report says every promise was kept in September. A letter on my desk says a daughter watched a frozen picture through her mother's committal.

blocks.text: I'm Yvaine, night director at Cadwallader's, a funeral home in an old mill town. At night I answer the phone when someone dies, and I sit with the people who come to us.

Since 2020 we have promised every family a live stream of the service. A camera in our chapel sends the picture over the internet as it happens, so relatives who cannot travel can watch from anywhere. The promise is printed on every order of service.

We don't run the stream ourselves. A company called Streamwell does, on its stream servers: computers that take our camera's picture and pass it on to everyone watching. Our contract says the stream will be up for 99.9% of the minutes in every month. If it isn't, Streamwell refunds 10% of that month's fee.
A promise like that, written into a contract with a price for breaking it, is called an SLA, short for service level agreement. Ours has never been broken.

September has 30 days: 43,200 minutes. Taking 99.9% of them leaves 43.2 minutes a month that the stream may be down without breaking the promise. That allowance is called the error budget. Like a month's pocket money, Streamwell may spend it however it likes.

Mostly it spends it on updates: new versions of its programs. An update goes in steps. First the new version installs for about half an hour while the old one keeps the stream going. Then the stream server restarts to switch over. For a few minutes, anyone watching sees a frozen picture. Then it moves again.

Until August, Streamwell started its updates at 02:00, so the restart came at about half past two, when nobody watches a funeral. On 1 September it moved them to 10:30 on weekdays, so that its staff are awake for them. It ran three in September. Our services start at 10:30 every weekday and last an hour; on busy days a second starts at 14:00. That made 31 services.

Streamwell's monthly report arrived at midnight on the 1st. Each line shows one figure: the minutes in the month, the minutes the stream was down, the percent up, the target, and the budget left in minutes.

STREAMWELL MONTHLY REPORT  Cadwallader's  September 2026
minutes in month    43,200
minutes down            26
percent up          99.94%
target               99.9%
budget left           17.2
status   every promise kept

On the desk, the day staff had left the post. One letter was from Albertine, who watched her mother's service on 24 September from a hospital bed abroad. The committal is the last goodbye, late in a service, when the curtain closes around the coffin. At 11:05, as the curtain began to move, her picture froze.
She watched a half-closed curtain for nine minutes. When the picture moved again, the curtain was closed and the chapel was emptying.

blocks.label: stream_24_september.png

diagram.aria: One hour, 24 September, 10:30 to 11:30. The service runs the whole hour. Streamwell's update installs from 10:30 to 11:05, then the stream server restarts and the stream is down from 11:05 to 11:14, 9 minutes. Markers: 11:05, the curtain begins to close and the picture freezes; 11:14, the picture moves again and the curtain is closed.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from Streamwell's log for 24 September. The update began installing at 10:30, as the service began. At 11:05 the stream server restarted, just as the curtain began to close, and the picture froze until 11:14. The report counted those 9 minutes against all 43,200 in the month.

blocks.text: The day staff had taken two calls about a frozen picture, on 8 and 16 September, and told both families it was probably their internet. Streamwell's log says it wasn't: 26 minutes down in September, all of them during three of our services.
Streamwell kept every word of its contract. What should we ask of it before the next family watches?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: I'm sorry for Albertine. Now look at what the report counts. The thing a promise measures is called an SLI, short for service level indicator. Yours counts every minute in the month, 43,200 of them, including half past two on a Sunday morning. How many of those minutes was a family watching? Add up your services. How many of those minutes were frozen, and what percent up is that? And where did August's restarts fall?

replies.author: u/cadwallader_nights_yvaine
replies.text: 31 services of an hour: 1,860 minutes when a service was live, being streamed to a family. I'll call them live minutes. 26 of them were frozen, so 98.6% up. August's restarts all came at about half past two in the morning, with no service live, and its report said 99.94% too.

comments.author: u/four_nines_valdemar
comments.text: 99.9% is a soft target: 43 minutes a month of nothing is a lot of nothing. Insist on four nines, 99.99%, in the next contract. That's 4.32 minutes a month. One nine-minute restart breaks it, so Streamwell pays every time, and a company that pays every time stops doing it. Four nines and this never happens.

comments.author: u/streamwell_theobald
comments.text: Theobald from Streamwell. I'm sorry for the family's loss, and for the picture. Inside Streamwell we set ourselves a target for every customer: the same 99.9% of minutes you see on the report. A target you set for yourself, with no price for missing it, is called an SLO, short for service level objective. We also keep a rule: once any customer's budget is spent, no more updates that month, except urgent fixes. In September no customer's budget ran out, and Cadwallader's had 17.2 minutes left, so the rule stopped nothing. Every one of our stream servers takes each update in the same minute, so they all run the same version.

comments.author: u/spare_everything_bathsheba
comments.text: Anything that matters needs a spare. Pay Streamwell for a second stream server, so while one is busy the other takes over within seconds, the way a hospital's generator starts when the mains fail. Taking over like that is called failover. One machine on its own is a single point of failure: when it stops, everything stops.

reply.prompt: October's services start on Thursday the 1st. What should Yvaine ask of Streamwell before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Ask for 99.99% of all minutes in the next contract, so the stream almost never drops.
options.verdict: Ten times stricter, just as blind
options.part2: First I replayed September in the sim at 99.99% of all minutes. The budget fell to 4.32 minutes. With Streamwell's rule off, the report said broken, 21.68 minutes over, 10% of the fee back, and the same three families watched a frozen picture. With the rule on, the 8 September update spent the whole budget at 11:04 in a service, and the other two were held. Then I moved the updates back to 02:00: the first still spent the budget, at half past two with nobody watching, and the other two were held anyway. The measure can't tell an empty night from a committal. Streamwell signed the new contract for a higher fee and kept its 10:30 updates. Its first October update froze a 10:30 service, and its rule then held every update for the rest of the month, a security fix among them.
options.senior: A stricter target on the wrong measure is still the wrong measure. Counting all minutes, a restart at half past two costs exactly what a restart during a committal costs, so the company has no reason to choose the night, and four nines only makes every minute dearer, the harmless ones too. Fix what you count before how much you demand. Targets above what people can notice also cost a great deal: Google's SRE book says 100% is probably never the right target.

options.text: Count only the minutes when a service is live, and hold Streamwell to that budget.
options.part2: In the sim I counted only live minutes: 31 services, 1,860 minutes, a budget of 1.86 at 99.9%. With the rule on, the 8 September update spent 9 live minutes and the rule held the other two: one family frozen instead of three, and the report said broken, 99.52%. With the updates at 02:00, or at 19:00 after every service, the same three cost no live minute: 100%, all 1.86 left, while the all-minutes report still said 99.94%. I sent Theobald the sums. Streamwell wrote 99.9% of live minutes into our contract, counted its budget rule on them, and moved its updates to 19:00, when its staff are still at work and no chapel it serves is open. In October no restart fell during a service, and no family wrote to us.
options.senior: Choose the SLI from what the people you serve feel, then set the target and the budget on it. A family feels only the minutes it is watching, so count those: good minutes over live minutes. On that measure September was 98.6%, a promise broken twice over, and the budget of 1.86 minutes makes a restart during a service impossible to afford, which is the point. The error budget then does its job: while it lasts, change freely; once it is spent, stop changing until it recovers. The same rule that stopped nothing on all minutes stops the right thing on live minutes.

options.text: Claim a refund for the three frozen services, and warn Streamwell in writing.
options.verdict: Fair to ask; nothing is owed
options.part2: I wrote to Streamwell claiming September's refund. Theobald answered the same day, politely: the contract refunds 10% only when a month falls below 99.9% of all minutes, and September was 99.94%, with 17.2 minutes to spare. The sim agreed: by the contract's own measure, refund none. My warning went into a file. Nothing in the contract changed, so nothing in Streamwell's schedule did. In October the updates still started at 10:30, and on a Tuesday another family's picture froze during the eulogy.
options.senior: An SLA's refund is a consequence, not a fix: it moves money after the harm and changes behaviour only if the harm shows up in the number. Here the number says the promise was kept, so a claim gets nothing and a warning changes nothing. Write it down, by all means, but change the measure the contract uses, or the company will keep meeting it while families keep missing goodbyes.

options.text: Pay for a second stream server, so one can take over while the other is being updated.
options.part2: We paid Streamwell for a second stream server. In the sim I switched the spare on and replayed September: still 26 minutes down, the same three families. Streamwell updates every server in the same minute, so the spare took the same update and restarted with the first; there was nothing left to take over. In October the 10:30 updates froze a service just as before, now on two servers at once, and our bill was higher.
options.senior: A spare protects against one machine breaking. It does nothing against a change made to every machine at once, because the change takes the spare down too. Failover helps when failures are independent; a shared update, a shared setting or a shared bug is a single point of failure that a second copy inherits. Look at what actually took the stream down before buying more of the thing that went down.

sim.title: Replay September at Cadwallader's
sim.lede: You're Yvaine at 00:00 on Tuesday 1 September 2026, before the first service. September has 30 days, 43,200 minutes. Cadwallader's holds 31 services, each streamed live for 60 minutes: one at 10:30 every weekday, and a second at 14:00 on the 1st, 3rd, 7th, 10th, 14th, 17th, 21st, 23rd and 28th, 1,860 live minutes in all. Streamwell runs three updates, on the 8th, 16th and 24th. Each installs for about half an hour from its start time; then the stream server restarts and the stream is down for 9, 8 and 9 minutes. Pick when updates start, what the promise counts (the SLI), the target, Streamwell's budget rule (hold updates once the budget is spent) and a second stream server, then replay the month a day or a week at a time.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press Next week, then Next day: on 8 September the stream is down 11:04 to 11:13, inside the 10:30 service. Run to the report: 26 minutes down, 99.94%, 17.2 left, kept, no refund, while by live minutes it is 98.6% and 3 of 31 services froze. Move updates to 02:00, as until August: the same 99.94%, and no service frozen. Back at 10:30, count live minutes: the budget is 1.86, the rule holds the 16th and 24th, and 1 service freezes. Try 19:00. Set 99.99% of all minutes with the rule on, at 02:00: two harmless updates held. Switch the second stream server on: nothing changes.

explain.oneLine: Nobody broke a promise. Streamwell's contract counted every minute in the month, so 26 minutes of restarts were 0.06% of 43,200 and left 17.2 minutes of budget. When the updates moved from 02:00 to 10:30, the same 26 minutes fell inside three services; counted over the 1,860 minutes families were watching, the stream was up 98.6%, and the measure could not see the difference.

steps.title: The promise counted every minute in the month.
steps.text: Streamwell's measure works in steps. First it counts the minutes in the month: 43,200 in September. Second it counts the minutes the stream was down: 26. Third it divides the good minutes by all the minutes: 43,174 of 43,200 is 99.94%. Fourth it compares that with the target, 99.9%, and prints kept or broken. Every step was right. What goes wrong sits in the first step: a minute at 03:00 on a Sunday counts exactly as much as the minute the curtain began to close. A thermometer in the hallway can say the house is warm while the bedroom is cold.

steps.title: The budget made 10:30 look as cheap as half past two.
steps.text: 99.9% of 43,200 minutes leaves an error budget of 43.2 minutes a month. A budget is meant to be spent, on updates and repairs, and Streamwell spent 26 of it. Before September its restarts came at about 02:30 and cost families nothing. In September they came a little after 11:00 and cost three families the end of a service. On the report both months look the same: 26 minutes, 99.94%, well inside the budget. A budget only steers spending if it is counted in the right currency.

steps.title: The minutes that matter are the live ones.
steps.text: An SLI should count what the people you serve feel. A family feels only the minutes it is watching: 31 services of an hour, 1,860 live minutes. Counted that way, 26 frozen minutes is 1.4% down, so 98.6% up, and a 99.9% target leaves a budget of 1.86 minutes a month. Google's SRE workbook suggests treating an SLI as good events divided by total events; here an event is a live minute, and a good one is a minute the picture moved. The 02:00 restarts cost nothing on this measure and the 10:30 ones break it, which is exactly what the families would say.

steps.title: SLA, SLO and the rule that stops changes.
steps.text: The SLA is the contract and its price: 10% of the fee back if the month falls below 99.9%. The SLO is the target Streamwell sets itself; teams usually set it a little tighter than the SLA, so they notice trouble before it costs money. The error budget turns the SLO into a rule for change. First, before each update, check the budget left. Second, if some is left, go ahead. Third, if it is spent, hold every change except urgent fixes. Fourth, start again when the next month's budget arrives. On all minutes the rule never fired. On live minutes it would have held the 16th and the 24th after the 8th spent the budget, and the next step is to move the updates where no service is live.

steps.title: Why the other fixes miss.
steps.text: Four nines of all minutes is a budget of 4.32 minutes, still blind to which minutes: it charges a harmless 02:30 restart the same as a committal, so it blocks good updates and gives no reason to move the bad ones. The refund follows the contract's own measure, which says the promise was kept, so nothing is owed. A second stream server protects against one machine breaking, but Streamwell updates every server in the same minute, so the spare restarts too. Each of these tightens or pays for the old measure; none changes what is counted.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for October. The chapel camera sends the live picture to Streamwell's stream servers, which stream it to the families watching: 1,860 live minutes a month. Streamwell's updates start at 19:00, after every service. The monthly report counts only live minutes against a budget of 1.86 minutes, and the budget rule stops updates once it is spent.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for October. The promise counts only the 1,860 minutes a service is live, so its budget is 1.86 minutes; Streamwell's updates start at 19:00, after every service, and its rule stops updates once that budget is spent. In the sim, September replayed this way freezes no service.

fix.title: The fix: count live minutes, and spend the budget on them
fix.text: Change what the promise counts. Make the SLI the minutes a service is live, and a good minute one where the picture moves: 1,860 live minutes in September. Keep 99.9% as the target, which leaves a budget of 1.86 minutes, and count Streamwell's own budget rule on the same minutes, so a restart during a service spends the budget and the next update waits. Write the measure into the contract, so the refund follows the same minutes. Streamwell then has every reason to restart when no service is live: at 19:00, with its staff still at work. Check it in the sim: live minutes, updates at 19:00, 0 services frozen, 1.86 left, while the all-minutes report still reads 99.94%.

limits: Counting live minutes at Streamwell's servers still misses a picture that leaves the server but stalls on the way to a family. Where you can, measure from the viewer's side: minutes that actually played on the family's screen.

A budget of 1.86 minutes leaves almost no room. One restart in a service breaks the month, so urgent security fixes need an agreed exception, and Streamwell needs a way to update without dropping a live stream.

Streamwell serves many homes, in more than one time zone. As it grows there may be no hour with no service live anywhere, so in time it must update one server at a time, moving live streams off each first.

head: What we ask
Good
Bad
rows: Simple to count; the contract has never been broken.
Blind to which minutes: 99.94% while 3 of 31 services froze.
Still blind: blocks harmless night updates and still freezes a service; costs more.
Nothing is owed by the contract's own measure; nothing changes.
Every server takes each update in the same minute, so the spare restarts too.
Counts what families feel; a budget of 1.86 makes restarts in services unaffordable.
Measured at the server, not the screen; needs an exception for urgent fixes.

explain.seniorTake: A reliability promise has three parts, and the first decides everything. The SLI is what you count; the SLO is the target you set yourself on it; the SLA is the contract that puts a price on missing it. Choose the SLI from what the people you serve feel, usually good events over valid events: requests that succeeded, minutes a stream moved while someone was watching. A measure that averages over time nobody uses will report a fine month while the people who matter have a terrible one, and every number downstream inherits the blindness: the budget, the rule, the refund. Then let the error budget steer change. While budget is left, ship; once it is spent, stop everything but urgent fixes until it recovers. That turns an argument between speed and safety into a number both sides agreed in advance. Set the SLO a little tighter than the SLA, so you act before it costs money, and resist targets near 100%: each nine costs far more than the one before, and past what people can notice it buys nothing.

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: SLI, SLO and SLA
realWorld.text: The chapter "Service Level Objectives" calls an SLI "a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided." "An SLO is a service level objective: a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI." An SLA is a contract "that includes consequences of meeting (or missing) the SLOs they contain."

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: what happens if it is missed
realWorld.text: "An easy way to tell the difference between an SLO and an SLA is to ask 'what happens if the SLOs aren't met?'" and "if there is no explicit consequence, then you are almost certainly looking at an SLO." Consequences are "most easily recognized when they are financial", such as a rebate or a penalty.

realWorld.title: Google SRE book: start from what users care about
realWorld.text: "Start by thinking about (or finding out!) what your users care about, not what you can measure." And on keeping a margin: "Using a tighter internal SLO than the SLO advertised to users gives you room to respond to chronic problems" before they become visible outside.

realWorld.title: Embracing Risk: the error budget
realWorld.text: The error budget "provides a clear, objective metric that determines how unreliable the service is allowed to be". "As long as there is error budget remaining", new releases can be pushed; if it is spent, "releases are temporarily halted while additional resources are invested" in reliability. The chapter adds that a 99.99% target "can be down for up to 52.56 minutes in a year", and that "100% is probably never the right reliability target".

realWorld.title: SRE workbook: good events over total events
realWorld.text: "Implementing SLOs" says "we generally recommend treating the SLI as the ratio of two numbers": "the number of good events divided by the total number of events." Its example policy includes "a production freeze halts certain changes to the system until there is sufficient error budget to resume changes", and "The error budget policy should also be documented".

asked: SLI, SLO, SLA: what is the difference?
What is an error budget for?
How would you choose an SLI for a video stream?
interview.answer: The SLI is the measurement: a number that says how well the service is doing, best written as good events over total events, such as requests that succeeded over all requests. The SLO is the target you set yourself on that measurement, say 99.9% over 30 days. The SLA is the contract with a customer that puts a consequence on missing a target, usually money back; the simplest test is to ask what happens if it is missed, and if nothing does, it is an SLO. Teams usually set the SLO a little tighter than the SLA, so they hear about trouble before it costs anything. The error budget is what the SLO leaves: at 99.9% over 43,200 minutes, 43.2 minutes of bad. It turns reliability into a shared decision rule: while budget is left, ship changes and take risks; when it is spent, freeze everything but urgent fixes until it recovers. For a video stream, I'd start from what a viewer feels, not from whether a server is up. Count only the minutes someone is watching, and call a minute good if the picture actually played: measured in the player if possible, since a server can be up while viewers stall. Then I'd add a couple more SLIs for quality, such as how long a stream takes to start and how often it stops to load. A story I'd tell: a funeral home's streaming contract promised 99.9% of all minutes in the month. When the provider moved its restarts from 02:00 to 10:30, the report still said 99.94% with 17.2 minutes of budget left, while 3 of 31 services froze, including a committal. Over the 1,860 minutes families were watching it was 98.6%. Counting live minutes made the budget 1.86 minutes, and the restarts moved to the evening.

terms.def: The funeral home in this story. Since 2020 it has promised every family a live stream of the service.
The funeral director on duty overnight: answers calls when someone dies and receives the people brought to the home.
The last goodbye near the end of a funeral service, when the coffin is committed to burial or cremation; at Cadwallader's, when the chapel curtain closes.
The printed sheet handed out at a funeral, listing the readings, music and words in order.
Sending a camera's picture over the internet as it happens, so people far away can watch at the same moment.
The streaming company in this story. It runs the stream servers that carry Cadwallader's services.
A computer (a server, s1e01) that takes the camera's picture and passes it on to everyone watching.
A new version of a company's programs. Streamwell's install for about half an hour, then the stream server restarts and the picture freezes for a few minutes.
Switching a program or computer off and on again, here to start the new version. While it restarts, it serves nobody.
Of the minutes counted, the share when the service worked: good minutes divided by all minutes counted, times 100. Also called availability.
A contract that promises a level of service and puts a price on missing it, such as 10% of the fee back. Streamwell's promises 99.9% of all minutes.
Money paid back when an SLA is missed; sometimes called a service credit or rebate. Streamwell's is 10% of that month's fee.
The percent up a promise aims for, such as 99.9%. What it leaves out is the error budget.
What a target leaves you to spend: at 99.9% of 43,200 minutes, 43.2 minutes down a month. Like pocket money for updates and repairs.
What a promise measures, best as good events over all events. Streamwell's counts every minute in the month; the fix counts live minutes.
The minutes when a service is being streamed to a family: 31 services of 60 minutes, 1,860 in September.
A target a team sets itself on an SLI, with no price for missing it. Usually a little tighter than the SLA, to give warning before it costs money.
An agreed rule for spending the error budget: while some is left, make changes; once it is spent, hold every change except urgent fixes until it refills.
A stop on changes to the live system, here until there is error budget again. The SRE workbook names it as one possible policy.
An urgent update that closes a weakness attackers could use. Budget rules usually let these through even when the budget is spent.
99.99%: four nines in a row. At four nines a 30-day month allows 4.32 minutes down; at three nines (99.9%), 43.2.
Another server ready to carry the stream if the first one fails. Streamwell updates every server in the same minute, so the spare restarts too.
A spare taking over when the main machine fails, ideally within seconds (s1e10). It helps only when the two don't fail together.
One part whose failure stops everything (s1e10). A change made to every server at once is one, even with spares.
The SRE workbook's way to write an SLI: the count of good events divided by the count of all events, such as minutes the picture moved over live minutes.
Streamwell's summary at midnight on the 1st: minutes in the month, minutes down, percent up, target, budget left.
A region that keeps the same clock time. A company serving several has no single quiet hour.
A practice scenario after s6e01 to s6e04 and s6e06: a retry storm that collapses without backoff and survives with it.
A hands-on project using s6e01, s6e05, s6e06 and s6e07: no false pages, SLOs for monitored sites, and an incident timeline.
An international standard for running information security. Its Annex A lists controls, among them A.5.20 to A.5.22 on suppliers.
The control for monitoring, review and change management of supplier services, so an agreed level of service delivery is kept.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria.
A SOC 2 availability criterion: the company maintains, monitors and evaluates current processing capacity and use of system components.

atWork: Look at every uptime number your company gives or receives: a supplier's monthly report, your own status page, an SLA in a contract. It is a common pattern for a supplier to meet its number while customers feel the outages, because the number counts the wrong minutes: all minutes in the month, or whether a server answered a check, rather than the minutes and requests customers actually used. Check three things. Does each SLI count good events over the events your users feel, such as successful requests or minutes a stream played while watched? Is the error budget counted on that same measure, with a written rule for what stops when it is spent? And does the contract's refund follow the same measure? Ask your suppliers when they make changes and whether a change can land in your busiest hour. Loadout L6 reuses this case, and Nightwatch N4 asks you to set SLOs for the sites it monitors. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, controls A.5.20 to A.5.22 cover supplier agreements and the monitoring, review and change management of supplier services, and an availability promise measured in the wrong minutes is exactly what a supplier review should catch; if it is pursuing SOC 2 availability, criterion A1.1 expects it to maintain, monitor and evaluate current processing capacity and use of system components. Choose the measures now, so the evidence exists before an auditor asks.

recall.prompt: Your company sells a parcel-tracking API to online shops. The contract promises 99.9% of the minutes in each month, and every monthly report says 99.95% or better. Your biggest customer says its checkout page breaks several times a week, always at about 14:00 on a weekday, its busiest hour. Your releases go out at 14:00 on weekdays, and each one takes the API down for about 2 minutes. What is wrong with how you measure, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The measure counts every minute the same, so outages in the busiest hour are diluted by quiet minutes
Choose an SLI that counts what customers feel, such as successful requests over all requests
Spend the error budget on that measure: stop or move releases when it is spent

recall.model: The report counts every minute the same, so 2 minutes down at the busiest hour weigh no more than 2 quiet minutes at 3 AM, and they are diluted across the whole month. Choose an SLI that counts what customers feel: successful requests over all requests, the good events over the total, so an outage at 14:00 counts for as many requests as it breaks. Set the SLO and the error budget on that measure. When the budget is spent, freeze releases until it recovers, and move the releases to a quiet hour so they stop spending it on checkouts.

recall.prompt: A promise says 99.9% of all minutes in a 30-day month. How many minutes may the service be down before the promise is broken?
recall.why: 30 days is 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of 43,200 is 43.2. That is the error budget. At 99.99% it would be 4.32, and at 99%, 432.

recall.prompt: Which of these comes with a consequence, such as money back, when it is missed?
recall.why: The SLA is the agreement with a customer, and it carries a consequence, usually a refund. The SLI is the measurement, the SLO is the target a team sets itself, and the error budget is what the target leaves. If nothing happens when it is missed, it is an SLO.

recall.prompt: 31 services are streamed for 60 minutes each. The stream is down for 26 minutes in the month, all during services. What percent up is that, counted over the minutes families were watching?
recall.why: 31 x 60 is 1,860 live minutes. 26 of 1,860 is 1.4% down, so 98.6% up. Counted over all 43,200 minutes in a 30-day month, the same 26 minutes look like 99.94%.

recall.prompt: What is a budget rule (an error budget policy) for?
options: To set the price of a refund in the contract
To decide in advance that changes stop once the budget is spent
To make sure the service is never down at all
To choose which minutes the promise counts
recall.why: The policy says what happens when the error budget runs out: changes stop, except urgent fixes, until there is budget again. The refund is the SLA's, the SLI chooses what is counted, and no rule makes a service never go down.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The live-minute promise works: since October Streamwell restarts at 19:00, and no family has written about a frozen picture. Until February. On 11 February six relatives wrote that the picture stuttered and stopped every few seconds through a whole 14:00 service. Streamwell's report for February says 100% of live minutes: its stream server sent the picture every minute of every service. The home's own internet line, which carries the camera's picture to Streamwell, was fine. Most of the six were watching on the same mobile network.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. How can the report say 100% while six families watched a stuttering picture, and what should the promise count now?

keyIdeas.idea: The SLI measures the server sending, not what reached the families' screens
Measure from the viewer's side: count minutes that actually played smoothly
Set the target and the error budget on that new measure

coldCase.model: The SLI counts what the stream server sent, the server side, not what reached the families' screens. The picture left Streamwell every minute and stalled on the way, on one mobile network, so the server's count was honest and the families' minutes were bad. Measure from the viewer's side: have each player report back, and count a live minute as good only if it played smoothly, without stalling, on the screens watching it. Then set the target and the error budget on those good minutes. A stall on one network may not be Streamwell's fault, so agree what the contract covers, but measure it anyway, because it is what the families saw.
